title: Microsoft Teams: identify external bots joining meetings
summary: Hold: the statement that no cap or budget control applies goes beyond Microsoft's documentation; an unpublished charge does not establish that conclusion. The policy paths, approval default and rollout details are supported, but the licensing description and a disagreement between Microsoft's PowerShell value lists need clarification.

claims.claim: Teams detects external meeting assistant bots attempting to join meetings hosted by the organisation.
claims.quote: Microsoft Teams provides admins with controls to detect and manage external bots when they attempt to join meetings hosted in their organization.

claims.claim: The roadmap describes clearly represented bots waiting in the lobby and organisers explicitly and separately admitting them if required.
claims.quote: Organizers will be required to explicitly and separately admit these bots into the meeting, if really required.

claims.where: front matter: defaultState; summary; What's changing; Why it matters; rationale
claims.claim: Bot detection is on by default for all tenants.
claims.quote: Bot detection will be enabled by default for all tenants. ... Keep the default setting, which requires organizers to approve detected bots before they join meetings (recommended).

claims.claim: The bot control is at Teams admin center > Meetings > Meeting policies > policy > Meeting join & lobby > Manage external bots and their access to meetings.
claims.quote: In the left navigation, select Meetings > Meeting policies. ... Select the policy you want to modify ... Under Meeting join & lobby, find Manage external bots and their access to meetings.

claims.claim: Set-CsTeamsMeetingPolicy -Identity <policy name> -ExternalBotAccessMode RequireApprovalWhenDetected sets detected-bot approval for the named policy.
claims.quote: Set-CsTeamsMeetingPolicy ... [[-Identity] <XdsIdentity>] ... [-ExternalBotAccessMode <String>] ... RequireApprovalWhenDetected: ... They will require approval before getting access to the meetings. This is the default value.

claims.claim: The lobby admission control is at Teams admin center > Meetings > Meeting policies > policy > Meeting join & lobby > Who can admit from lobby.
claims.quote: In the Teams admin center, expand Meetings and then select Meeting policies. ... Select the policy that you want to update. ... In the Meeting join & lobby sections, update the settings ... Who can admit from lobby

claims.claim: Set-CsTeamsMeetingPolicy -Identity <policy name> -UsersCanAdmitFromLobby OrganizerAndCoOrganizersOnly sets the lobby admission default to organisers and co-organisers.
claims.quote: You can use the Set-CsTeamsMeetingPolicy PowerShell cmdlet ... To control who can admit users from the lobby, use the -UsersCanAdmitFromLobby parameter. ... Only allow organizers and co-organizers to admit participants from the lobby ... OrganizerAndCoOrganizersOnly

claims.claim: Learn documents three options: do not detect bots, require approval when detected, and block all detected bots.
claims.quote: Do not detect bots ... When detected, require approval before joining (default) ... Block all detected bots

claims.claim: The other PowerShell values on the feature's Learn page are BlockDetectedBots and AllowBots.
claims.quote: Do not detect bots | AllowBots ... Block all detected bots | BlockDetectedBots
claims.fix: Replace the note's first sentence with 'The feature page lists BlockDetectedBots and AllowBots; the Set-CsTeamsMeetingPolicy reference instead names AllowAllBots for disabling detection.' Both URLs are already cited: https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoftteams/manage-external-bots and https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoftteams/set-csteamsmeetingpolicy?view=teams-ps.

claims.where: controls[0].note; What's changing; Scope; Governance controls
claims.claim: The bot policy setting applies to meetings hosted by users assigned that policy.
claims.quote: The setting applies to meetings hosted by users assigned the meeting policy.

claims.where: What's changing; Risk assessment; rationale: risk
claims.claim: With approval required, detected bots wait in the lobby regardless of the meeting's lobby configuration.
claims.quote: Detected bots are placed in the meeting lobby regardless of the meeting's lobby configuration.

claims.claim: Registered bots appear in the lobby's Waiting section.
claims.quote: In the meeting lobby, registered bots appear in the Waiting section

claims.claim: Unverified bots detected by Teams appear under Suspected threats.
claims.quote: unverified bots detected through behavioral and infrastructure signals appear under Suspected threats.

claims.claim: Block all detected bots automatically blocks detected bots rather than asking an organiser to admit them.
claims.quote: Detected bots are automatically blocked from joining the meeting. They aren't placed in the meeting lobby for organizer approval, and meeting organizers can't admit them.

claims.claim: Do not detect bots leaves bots unmarked and subject to existing participant access and lobby settings.
claims.quote: Bots aren't detected or marked in the lobby or in the meeting. They appear as any other external participant in the meetings and follow the meeting's existing access and lobby settings.

claims.where: What's changing; Why it matters; Risk assessment; rationale: risk
claims.claim: Detection can miss bots, which continue to be governed by existing meeting access settings.
claims.quote: Some bots may not be detected and may continue to join meetings according to existing meeting access settings.

claims.where: What's changing; Risk assessment: Security & identity
claims.claim: Detection can incorrectly flag a human participant as a bot.
claims.quote: Detection may incorrectly identify a human participant as a bot.

claims.claim: Blocking can prevent wrongly flagged participants from joining.
claims.quote: Participants incorrectly identified as bots may be prevented from joining the meeting. Where supported, eligible participants can use the email verification recovery experience to verify their identity and attempt to join.

claims.claim: Block all detected bots does not guarantee that all external bots are blocked.
claims.quote: The Block all detected bots option applies to bots identified by Teams detection mechanisms. It does not guarantee that all external bots will be blocked.

claims.where: Risk assessment: Security & identity; What's changing; Why it matters; controls[1].governs
claims.claim: Organisers, and presenters depending on the meeting setting, explicitly admit detected bots under the approval option.
claims.quote: Organizers (also presenters, depending on the meeting setting), need to explicitly admit these bots into the meeting.

claims.claim: Who can admit from lobby defaults to Organizers and presenters.
claims.quote: When set to its default value of Organizers and presenters, only organizers and presenters can admit participants into the meeting from the lobby.

claims.claim: Who can admit from lobby sets a default that organisers can change through Meeting options.
claims.quote: This policy sets a default that your organizers can change through their Meeting options.

claims.where: Risk assessment: Change & support; Governance guidance
claims.claim: Under approval required, organisers can admit wrongly flagged people and use This is not a bot to correct their representation.
claims.quote: Organizers can admit the participant from the lobby and use the This is not a bot option to correct the participant's representation in that meeting.

claims.where: Risk assessment: Change & support; Governance guidance
claims.claim: Microsoft asks users to report undetected bots through the Feedback option in Teams.
claims.quote: Help improve the system by reporting any undetected external meeting bots to us via the Feedback option in Teams.

claims.claim: External meeting bots can record or transcribe meetings.

claims.where: front matter: licensing.model; Cost and licensing; rationale: cost; Open questions
claims.claim: The licensing model is unknown because no licence specific to bot detection has been published.
claims.quote: Except for joining Teams meetings anonymously, each user in your organization must have a Teams license before they can use Teams.
claims.fix: Set licensing.model to included. Replace the licensing notes and the first licensing paragraph with 'A Microsoft Teams license is required for each user in the organisation to use Teams, except for joining meetings anonymously. Microsoft has not published a licence or meter specific to bot detection as of November 2026.' Cite https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoftteams/user-access. In the cost rationale replace 'A licence statement is not yet published' with 'No feature-specific licence or meter is published.' Replace the first open question with 'Will Microsoft publish any licence or meter specific to bot detection? Watch the Learn page and MC1251206.'

claims.where: licensing.notes; Cost and licensing; rationale: cost
claims.claim: The feature's Learn page and MC1251206 name no licence, meter or charge specific to bot detection.
claims.quote: Searched: Teams external bot detection license ExternalBotAccessMode pricing; Teams licensing meetings. Read manage-external-bots, MC1251206, user-access and Teams add-on licenses; read Premium licensing search excerpts. No bot-detection licence, meter or charge found.

claims.claim: No cap or budget control applies because no charge is documented.
claims.quote: Searched: "external bots" "budget" "Teams" spending cap; Teams external bot detection license pricing budget. Read manage-external-bots, Teams add-on licenses and user-access; searches found no statement that no cap or budget control applies to detection.
claims.fix: Remove 'No cap or budget control applies, because no charge is documented.' The narrower statement that no feature-specific meter or charge is published is already covered by the licensing paragraph.
